entries.name: Pharos of Alexandria
entries.era: c. 297-283 BCE to medieval collapse (earthquakes, 1303 and 1323 CE)
entries.purpose: guiding light for shipping into the Great Harbour of Alexandria
parts: great mirror (said to burn enemy ships, probably legend)
layout: three-tiered tower on the islet of Pharos at the mouth of the harbour
linked to the mainland by the Heptastadion causeway
light visible far out to sea by day (white marble glare) and night (fire)
entries.found: at Alexandria, Egypt; one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world
entries.notes: Height figures vary (100-137 m); every medieval travel writer left a different number. Built by Sostratus of Cnidus for Ptolemy I/II.

entries.name: Carthaginian cothon (naval harbour)
entries.purpose: hidden military harbour; Carthage's war fleet laid up under cover
parts: outer rectangular commercial harbour next door
layout: dead-circular basin, unlike any other ancient naval harbour
island in the middle with the admiralty; sheds ring the water on both inner faces
entrance narrow enough to block with a ship and a chain
entries.found: at Carthage (near Tunis); excavated in the 20th century, partially reconstructable from Appian and archaeology
entries.notes: Most distinctive harbour plan ever built: the enemy fleet sees nothing until the boom drops. Sheds held ~220 warships (Appian's figure).

entries.name: Arsenal of Venice
entries.purpose: industrial dockyard for building, arming and outfitting the Venetian fleet
parts: great gate (Porta Magna, 1460) with lions from Greece
layout: walled complex, off-limits to citizens; largest industrial site in medieval Europe
ships moved through successive basins; hull, masting, rigging, armament in sequence
standardized parts and assembly-line method centuries before Ford
entries.found: in Venice, northeast of the city centre; still a working (now mostly decommissioned) naval zone
entries.notes: Covers ~48 ha. Dante compared it to Hell with the pitch boiling; by 1500 it could launch a galley a day on ceremony.

entries.name: Harbour boom chain (Golden Horn)
entries.purpose: blocking an enemy fleet from entering a harbour or strait
parts: floats of wood to keep the chain awash
towers at each shore with windlasses
stone piers at the water ends
layout: strung across the mouth of the Golden Horn from the Acropolis to Galata
sits at water level; galleys cannot ram through; small boats pass if chain lowered
entries.found: at Constantinople (717 vs the Arabs, 1203-04 vs the Fourth Crusade, 1453 vs the Ottomans); similar chains protected Tyre, Alexandria, New York (War of 1812), Sydney
entries.notes: Failed in 1453 only because Mehmed II dragged his ships overland on greased logs into the Horn.

entries.name: Medieval treadwheel harbour crane
entries.purpose: lifting cargo between quay and ship
parts: rope wound on the wheel axle
layout: mounted on the quay edge, often on a stone base projecting over the water
two dockers walk inside the treadwheel to raise the load
some are slewing cranes on a pivot; the earliest sit inside crane houses (Cologne, Antwerp, Gdansk, Bruges, Lisbon)
entries.found: major medieval ports: Antwerp (still standing), Cologne, Gdansk, Bruges, Lisbon; a few survive as museums
entries.notes: Lifts 2-4 t. A direct ancestor of the dockside crane; the treadwheel is the same machine as the medieval siege hoist.

entries.name: Tidal fish weir (stake weir)
entries.purpose: trapping fish at low tide in a walled enclosure on the flats
parts: V- or heart-shaped wall open to the sea
layout: built across tidal flats or estuaries, exposed at low water
wings guide fish toward a narrow trap they cannot escape on the ebb
visible only from above at low tide or as lines of stakes at high tide
blueprint: legend: w stone/brush wall trap, . water or wet sand; walls lead fish to the centre pound
entries.found: every tidal coast: Roman sites on the North Sea, medieval ones in England (mentioned in Domesday), Aboriginal stone traps on the Australian coast, Japanese ama fishing grounds
entries.notes: Cheap to build, free to run, needs a big tide range. Ideal low-effort shore economy in a coastal starter village.

entries.name: Lazaretto (quarantine station)
entries.purpose: isolating crews, passengers and cargo from plagued ships before they enter port
parts: quarantine sheds for goods (quaranta giorni, 40 days)
layout: built on a small offshore island to cut the water route to the mainland
strict one-way flow: suspect cohorts in, disinfected goods out
first lazaretto: Santa Maria di Nazareth island (Venice, 1423); Dubrovnik's 1377 edict invented the 40-day quarantine
entries.found: Venice (Lazzaretto Vecchio and Nuovo), Dubrovnik, Marseille, Genoa, Malta, Sydney; many linger as derelict islands near old ports
entries.notes: The original public-health cordon: a whole island needed to stop the plague by ship. Great atmospheric ruin site for a port city.

entries.name: Thames Barrier
entries.purpose: keeping North Sea storm surges out of the tidal Thames and Greater London
parts: 4 large rising sector gates (61 m span)
layout: spans the Thames at Woolwich Reach, 520 m wide
gates lie flat in sills when open (ships pass over), rotate upright to close (holds back 5 m+ surge)
designed for 1-in-1000 annual surge risk
entries.found: at Woolwich Reach, London; visible from both banks as rows of hood-shaped piers
entries.notes: One of the largest movable flood barriers in the world. Closed 200+ times since 1982; every closure is a real event in the port's calendar.

entries.name: La Rance tidal power station
entries.purpose: generating electricity from the 13 m tide of the Rance estuary
layout: crosses the Rance estuary between Saint-Malo and Dinard
turbines generate on both ebb and flood tides
doubled as a crossing; road traffic shares the deck
entries.found: on the Rance estuary, Brittany; the world's first large tidal barrage and largest for decades (still among the biggest by capacity factor)
entries.notes: Best tidal range in Europe made the Rance the obvious first site; the barrage also tamed the estuary's bores.

entries.name: Panama Canal
entries.purpose: linking the Atlantic and Pacific across the Isthmus of Panama
parts: Pedro Miguel and Miraflores Locks (Pacific side)
Gatun Lake (artificial, 26 m above sea level)
Culebra (Gaillard) Cut through the Continental Divide
layout: 82 km cutting through mountains; all ships climb 26 m and descend by lock steps
the French sea-level attempt failed on yellow fever; the American lock design succeeded
expansion (2016) added a third lane of larger locks (Neopanamax)
entries.found: across the Isthmus of Panama; about 140 km of transit including approach channels
entries.notes: Saves ~15,000 km by water versus rounding Cape Horn. One lock chamber is a perfect 1:1 voxel scale for a 200 m x 20 m gate.

entries.name: Suez Canal
entries.purpose: sea-level waterway linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea
parts: Great and Small Bitter Lakes (water reservoir)
Port Said and Port Tewfik terminals
layout: straight-ish trench through the Egyptian desert, no locks (sea-level design)
widened and deepened repeatedly; modern depth ~24 m for fully laden 24,000-TEU ships
entries.found: from Port Said (Mediterranean) to Suez (Red Sea); current handles ~10% of world trade
entries.notes: The Ever Given grounding (March 2021) blocked the canal for 6 days; the whole world noticed. Useful scale reference for any desert coast scene.

entries.name: Dry dock
entries.era: c. 400 BCE (Piraeus naval docks) to now
entries.purpose: repairing and building ships below the waterline in the dry
parts: caisson or gate at the sea end
keel blocks along the centre line
layout: aligned with a sheltered reach of coast or harbour mouth
ship floats in over the keel blocks, gate shuts, water pumped out
Great Harry's dock at Portsmouth (1495) is the surviving early example; Greek Zea naval docks are older
entries.found: every major warship and repairing port; the word 'dockyard' derives from it
entries.notes: A whole ship sits on blocks below the harbour floor: the best dramatic reveal a port city can have.

entries.name: Slipway (marine railway / gridiron)
entries.purpose: hauling small craft out of the water for repairs
parts: winch or capstan at the top
layout: ramp runs from above high-water mark down below low tide
boat slides down on launch, hauled up on ways for repair
careening for hull cleaning is the oldest version, done at neap tides on a beach
entries.found: small boatyards, fishing harbours, lifeboat stations
entries.notes: Careening beaches are still used; a grounded caravel is a very plausible 15th-century scene.

entries.name: Bell buoy
entries.era: 19th century to now (unlit predecessors from antiquity)
entries.purpose: marking hazards and channel edges by sound when the sea moves the float
parts: bell on a yoke that swings with the waves
mooring chain to a seabed sinker
layout: moored at a fixed point; only the float is visible at the surface
lanby (light vessel) buoys are larger relatives protecting lightships' stations
entries.found: every navigable coast and river approach; red/green lateral marks at channel sides
entries.notes: The smallest maritime structure and the easiest to miss. Two or three along a channel entrance read instantly as 'shipping here'.

entries.name: Leading marks (leading lights)
entries.purpose: two lights in line showing the safe line through a channel (range lights)
layout: two towers of different heights on the same bearing from seaward
navigator lines them up; if one is offset, the ship is off the fairway
daymarks are often striped or patterned boards rather than lights
entries.found: channel entrances, bar crossings, river mouths with shifting shoals; lights at Lynn, Zeebrugge, and countless harbour bars
entries.notes: Cheapest accurate navigation aid ever: two lamps on the right bearing. A pair of striped towers reads clearly at voxel scale.

entries.name: Trireme
entries.purpose: fast oared warship; ramming weapon, not a cargo carrier
parts: trireme hull (3 levels of oars, 170 rowers)
mast with square sail (stepped ashore in battle)
layout: long, narrow, almost flush-decked; no castles fore or aft
oars in three superimposed tiers, 85 per side
fought under oar power near shore; slow under sail
entries.found: classical Mediterranean; Battle of Salamis (480 BCE) was fought by them
entries.notes: At voxel scale: one and a half building lots long, nothing else like it in profile. 170 rowers means the crew is a crowd.

entries.name: Viking longship
entries.purpose: fast warship and troop transport; beach-anywhere raider
parts: carved bow and stern posts (dragon heads on great ships)
layout: long, shallow, symmetric bow and stern - can reverse direction without turning
sails on open sea, rows upriver; lands anywhere a beach permits
Gokstad ship (~23 m) and Oseberg ship (~21 m) are the type fossils
entries.found: Scandinavia and Viking expansion lands; found as burial ships in Norwegian fjords
entries.notes: Drakkars raided from Lindisfarne (793) to L'Anse aux Meadows. The ~1 m draft is the whole design secret.

entries.name: Cog (Hanseatic cargo ship)
entries.purpose: bulk cargo carrier of the Hanseatic League: grain, timber, salt, fish
parts: straight sternpost with stern rudder (replacing side steering oars)
high fore and aft castles (added for defence)
layout: beamy, bluff-bowed tub of a ship; trades honesty for capacity
one mast, one sail, crew of ~15-20
remains the archetype of the medieval merchantman
entries.found: North Sea and Baltic; wrecks (Bremen cog, 1380s) preserved in museums
entries.notes: 200 tonnes deadweight with 15 sailors - astonishing economy. The straight stem is an easy voxel silhouette.

entries.name: Dhow (Arabian/Indian Ocean sailing ship)
entries.purpose: monsoon-following cargo trade across the Indian Ocean
parts: lateen (settee) sail, one or two masts
sewn-plank or nailed hull (no iron nails in the classic build)
layout: sails with the monsoons: out in winter (to India), home in summer
rice, dates, horses, ivory and spices moved this way for a millennium
baghla and boom are the big Arab types (30-40 m); smaller sambuk and zaruq for coasts
entries.found: from Zanzibar to Muscat to Gujarat; still the working ship of the Gulf and East Africa
entries.notes: Sewn hulls flex without working loose; timber choice tracked the monsoon route. Ideal trading vessel for a non-European coast.

entries.name: Junk (Chinese sailing ship)
entries.purpose: bulk cargo and treasure transport; the great ship of the Asian seas
parts: battened junk sail (reefs from the deck by lowering)
layout: bluff hull, multi-masted, fan-like sails with bamboo battens
Chinese sources describe treasure ships over 100 m under Zheng He (early 1400s) - the scale is disputed but ordinary merchant junks ran 30-45 m
entries.found: China coast, Taiwan, Southeast Asia; Zheng He's treasure voyages reached Arabia and East Africa (1405-1433)
entries.notes: Bulkheads made junks unsinkable by principle: a holed compartment is just one wet room. The European barque borrowed the rudder from China via the Indian Ocean.

entries.name: Caravel
entries.purpose: exploration and dispatch; shallow-draft, weatherly, fast
parts: lateen (la Latina) or square (la Redonda) rig
layout: small enough for a crew of 20-25; shallow draft runs up rivers
lateen rig sailed closer to the wind - the key to beating home from Africa
Niña and Pinta were caravels; Santa Maria was a nao, not a caravel
entries.found: Iberian expansion; Prince Henry's exploration down the West African coast; Columbus 1492
entries.notes: 20 m of ship that opened two oceans' knowledge. The iconic 'Age of Discovery' hull.

entries.name: Galleon
entries.purpose: heavily armed sailing warship and treasure carrier
parts: three or four masts: square courses forward, lateen mizzen aft
layout: long, narrow gun platform; firepower forward and aft but decisive broadside
Manila galleons ran the Acapulco-Manila route 1565-1815; Spanish Armada (1588) was galleons and carracks
entries.found: Atlantic approaches, Caribbean convoys, the Manila trade
entries.notes: Sun-gilded sterns, rated in guns, sunk by storms more often than battles. San Juan de Ulúa (1568) shows the type arming up at anchor for a famous fight.

entries.name: Clipper
entries.purpose: fastest sailing cargo ships ever; first to market with tea, wool, sugar
parts: sharp, yacht-like hull with enormous sail area
very fine entry and long overhanging counter
layout: flogged for speed: speed = first premium on cargo, so hull form chased records
Cutty Sark (85 m, 1869) is the surviving specimen; Thermopylae (1868) her great rival
tea from Foochow to London in ~100-110 days was the contest
entries.found: China-England tea run, Australia-England wool run, California gold rush
entries.notes: Waterline fineness at the entry is the whole design: knives through the sea at 14+ knots. Last gasp of commercial sail before steam.

entries.name: Polynesian double-hulled voyaging canoe
entries.era: c. 1500 BCE-1200 CE (voyage era); revived with Hokule'a 1976
entries.purpose: two-way ocean voyaging carrying 20-40 people, plants and animals between islands
layout: double hulls with the load on the platform; no keel, needs a navigator of star lore and wave reading
settlement of Remote Oceania (Fiji-Tonga-Samoa to Hawaii, Rapa Nui, New Zealand) was done aboard these
Hokule'a (1976) recreated the route Hawaii-Tahiti; her sister Hikianalia continues it
entries.found: Polynesia: Hawaii, Samoa, Tonga, Tahiti, New Zealand, Rapa Nui; built today by revival crews
entries.notes: The most audacious ocean crossing ever sailed from known to unknown. The whole exploration of the Pacific fits in one 20-metre hull pair.

entries.name: Paddle steamer
entries.purpose: scheduled passenger and cargo service where sail failed - rivers, estuaries, coastal routes
layout: shallow-draft for rivers (Mississippi, Lower Rhine, Clyde); SS Great Western (1838) was the ocean-going version
wheelboxes and crossed funnels make the silhouette unmistakable
raced with sail packets for speed records on major routes
entries.found: Mississippi and Ohio rivers, Clyde and Thames excursions, transatlantic crossings (until screw propulsion took over in the 1860s)
entries.notes: The first machine-age silhouette on the water. Great period atmosphere for an 1830s-1880s port.

entries.name: Container ship (post-Panamax)
entries.era: 1956 (Ideal X, first container sailing) to now
entries.purpose: moving standardised 20/40-ft containers between hub ports
parts: cell guides for stacking to deck
single big diesel (or until recently, HFO)
adjoined accommodation block, all cargo forward/ aft
layout: riding high with containers stacked 8-10 abreast to deck edge and one to two tiers above
capacity 13,000 to 24,000 TEU; Ever Given 20,000+
sails at ~22 knots on fixed pendulum schedules
entries.found: every major trade lane; the Ever Given's March 2021 blockage of the Suez was the defining image of container trade
entries.notes: At voxel scale this is a cliff of coloured boxes: the scale problem becomes the whole scene. A single ship is a moving city block.

entries.name: Fish aggregating device (FAD)
entries.era: antiquity to now (motorised drifting FADs from the 20th century)
entries.purpose: attracting pelagic fish (tuna, mahi-mahi) to a known point for purse seining or handlining
parts: surface float of buoy/raft or clustered fronds
top float with flag or light (modern)
layout: anchored raft or drifting tangle of stems 100-1000 m offshore
bait fish shelter under it; tuna follow within hours
traditional Pacific rig: coconut fronds tied round a log; modern: satellite-tracked plastic rafts
entries.found: tropical seas everywhere; village tuna FADs anchor offshore in Pacific island EEZs
entries.notes: The cheapest marine structure that exists; invisible until you know to look. A fisherman's secret spot is a single object in the blue.

entries.name: Oyster raft (hanging culture)
entries.purpose: growing oysters suspended in the water column below a floating raft
layout: parallel rafts in a sheltered, plankton-rich bay
oysters hang 2-8 m deep; raft moves with the tide
Hiroshima raft culture is the canonical example; French tables (tables sur sol) are the shore equivalent
entries.found: sheltered bays with plankton: Hiroshima, Brittany, Zeeland, Chesapeake (rack culture)
entries.notes: Low tide reveals acres of poles and floats in straight rows - the signature of any productive mollusc coast.

entries.name: Bouchot mussel poles
entries.purpose: growing mussels on intertidal poles in sheltered flats
parts: poles ~4-7 m high, driven in rows
coiled rope sleeves for mussel seed
star-shaped tables at low tide for training
layout: long rows of poles marching across the tidal flats, parallel to the shore
rows are straight enough to navigate; harvested on foot at low tide
coir rope seeded in spring, mussels grown 12-18 months
entries.found: Brittany and Normandy (Mont-Saint-Michel Bay is the classic landscape)
entries.notes: A forest of poles at low tide and invisible at high: the coast literally grows. A strong biome-specific scene for France.

entries.name: Pearl oyster farm (grafting rafts)
entries.purpose: growing and grafting Pinctada maxima/penguin/margaritifera for cultured pearls
parts: longline or raft grids with hanging nets
layout: rafts in a sheltered lagoon with clean, warm water
Oysters are seeded at 1-2 years, grafted at 2-3, harvested at 5-7
Ago Bay (Mikimoto's first site) and Garaffi/Gambier (French Polynesia) are the famous ones
entries.found: Ago Bay (Japan), Gambier Islands and Tuamotus (French Polynesia), Broome approach (Australia)
entries.notes: Ten pearls from a thousand grafted oysters is a good year. A small, exquisite industry - very different in mood from a fish cannery.

entries.name: Salmon net pen (sea cage)
entries.purpose: farming Atlantic salmon in sea water for 2-3 years before harvest
layout: groups of 6-12 circular cages in a sheltered fjord or bay
automated feeding from a barge; divers net-clean monthly
escapes and sea lice are the industry's twin headaches
entries.found: Norway fjords, Scotland west coast, Chile (Chiloé), Canadian BC, Tasmania
entries.notes: A cage of 200,000 salmon is a farm you can stand on the deck of. The coastline looks 'stocked' in a very distinctive way.

entries.name: Seaweed farm (nori/kelp lines)
entries.era: c. 1670 (nori in Tokyo Bay first recorded) to now
entries.purpose: growing nori, wakame, kombu or dulse for food, carrageenan and alginate
parts: bamboo or plastic poles in rows
layout: grid of poles in shallow sheltered water, waist-deep at low tide
nets seeded with spores in summer, harvested in winter
China grows more kelp than anywhere; Japan/Korean nori dominates the food market
entries.found: Tokyo Bay and Ariake Sea (Japan), Yellow Sea (China/Korea), Brittany (France), Maine (US)
entries.notes: At low tide the farm is a dark grid on the flats; at high tide, invisible. A good 'alive' coastal scene with minimal machinery.

entries.name: Shore whaling station
entries.era: c. 1900-1965 (modern era); Basque whaling from the 11th century
entries.purpose: flensing and processing whales caught by catcher boats
layout: slipway aligned with the deep-water approach; carcass hauled up and stripped
tryworks reduces blubber to oil in continuous cookers
Grytviken, South Georgia (1904, Carl Anton Larsen) is the example; all closed by the 1965 factory-ship ban
entries.found: South Georgia, Iceland, Norway, Newfoundland; now derelict or museum sites
entries.notes: An abandoned whaling station is the archetypal maritime ruin: huge slipway, rusted boilers, mountains of bone.

entries.name: Coastal salt pans (salterns)
entries.purpose: evaporating sea water to harvest salt
layout: sequence of progressively saltier ponds stair-stepped from the sea
brine spends weeks in the first ponds, days in the last; salt is raked in summer
Aigues-Mortes (France, 13th c.) and the salterns of Brittany and Portugal still operate
entries.found: every warm, dry, low coast: Mediterranean, Iberia, Brittany (fleur de sel), China, India
entries.notes: White geometric ponds from the air; a living industry older than Rome. Water colour shifts pink-purple with brine shrimp - great for map art.

entries.name: Tombolo (sand or shingle causeway to an island)
entries.era: formed since sea level stabilised after the last ice age
entries.purpose: natural land connection between mainland and island (e.g. Chesil Beach-Portland)
layout: long narrow ridge of pebbles, arcuate in plan
Chesil Beach: 29 km long, up to 15 m high, 200 m wide at the base
forms where longshore drift builds a spit across an island's lee shadow
entries.found: Chesil Beach (Dorset, England), Mont-Saint-Michel (tidal causeway approaches), Saint-Nazaire causeway (Brittany)
entries.notes: A natural 29-km breakwater. Walking the Fleet lagoon at low tide is one of Europe's stranger landscapes.

entries.name: Barrier island
entries.era: forming for the last ~6,000-8,000 years of sea-level stability
entries.purpose: a wave-built sand ridge protecting the lagoon/estuary behind from the open sea
layout: long narrow sand ridge parallel to the mainland shore
cut by tidal inlets which migrate over decades
the US East/Gulf coast is one long chain: Outer Banks, Florida barrier islands, Mississippi-Alabama chain
entries.found: passive margins: US East and Gulf coasts, the Wadden Sea barrier chain (Holland-German-Danish), West Africa, Queensland
entries.notes: The reason every low coast has a sheltered lagoonside village; the islands move landward as sea level rises.

entries.name: Tidal flat (mudflat/sandflat)
entries.purpose: intertidal plain exposed twice daily; habitat for worms, shellfish, wading birds
parts: fine laminae of mud and sand
layout: vast, nearly flat expanse, inundated at high tide
highest biological productivity per area on Earth after rainforests
the Wadden Sea (Netherlands-Germany-Denmark, ~10,000 km²) is the world's largest continuous system
entries.found: Wadden Sea, Morecambe Bay, Wash, estuaries everywhere with fine sediment and big tides
entries.notes: The landscape that most resembles a game's flat 'low tide' mode; a feeding ground for the world's migratory shorebirds.

entries.name: Salt marsh
entries.era: forming continuously where sheltered flats accumulate sediment
entries.purpose: intertidal grassland trapping sediment and damping storm waves
parts: high marsh (flood on spring tides only)
layout: behind barrier islands and in estuaries; drained by winding creeks
green-black, flat, bisected by shining creeks; mosquitoes and waders
turns sea salt into peat - a carbon store built in plain sight
entries.found: every temperate coast with sheltered flats: US East coast, North Sea, New Zealand, Patagonia
entries.notes: The cheapest storm-surge defence ever devised, free. Spartina anglica transformed the British coast in the 19th century.
